A1.notes.Q3: Basic performance data is standard, but I need a tangible benefit to justify it. Disability status might be the only exception where transparency on help matters most.
A1.notes.Q4: Students need to know exactly why they are contacted, especially if the contact involves an advisor or sensitive support options.
A1.notes.Q5: If we miss a student in crisis because of unfairness, that harm outweighs efficiency. Prioritizing recall for all groups is crucial here.
A1.notes.Q6: I prefer proactive support over waiting for requests, but the intervention style must not feel like surveillance.
A1.notes.Q7: For generic emails, cast a wider net; for personalized advisor contact, precision is vital to avoid disrupting students' lives unnecessarily.
A1.Q8.1: We must ensure the 'support offered' doesn't become bureaucratic overhead that delays actual help reaching vulnerable groups.

A2.notes.Q3: I find course grades essential (Q3.2). Admissions data helps see potential but raises stakes, so higher threshold needed (Q3.3). Activity logs feel intrusive like surveillance; I need a large improvement to accept them.
A2.notes.Q4: Without clear explanations, students won't trust the flag for support (my own students often argue against it). I can only accept complex models if they catch many more at-risk kids than we miss now.
A2.notes.Q5: Unfairness is unacceptable to me as an advisor; it discriminates against specific groups. However, if fairness means missing fewer false positives (harassing innocent students), I accept a small overall efficiency loss rather than more errors.
A2.notes.Q6: Emails are low burden; personalized messages feel more caring but require resources. No need for calls unless flagged repeatedly, to avoid over-contacting.

A3.notes.Q3: Credits and grades are essential for me to assess progress, so a moderate improvement threshold makes sense here. Admissions data helps identify students at risk of failing too early on their program track; however, adding Absalon activity (page views) feels like surveillance that crosses ethical lines unless the model is perfect.
A3.notes.Q4: High explainability is crucial for building trust with students who might feel targeted unfairly by a black box algorithm. However, given the goal of proactive support rather than judgmental decision-making, I would accept a drop to low or very-low explainability only if it significantly improves our ability to catch struggling students we currently miss.
A3.notes.Q5: Missing a student who needs help is worse than sending an unwanted email, which I can handle as a advisor but cannot mitigate the risk of a student dropping out because they felt targeted and ignored.
A3.notes.Q6: I prefer personalized outreach; generic emails often go unopened, whereas personal contact from an advisor signals genuine care rather than a robotic system attempt to intervene.
A3.Q8.1: We need clear guidelines so advisors know when they should escalate flagged students immediately versus deferring action if follow-up shows no acute risk. We don't want alert fatigue preventing us from reaching out to those in genuine crisis.

S1.notes.Q3: I've already dropped out, so early detection feels critical to me anyway. Disability data is vital for support; age/gender/nationality feel intrusive unless they directly help prevent future drops like mine.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly what caused my flagging before trusting the system or asking for help, but if it misses me at this point of low explainability, I won't use it.
S1.notes.Q5: It shouldn't penalize students from similar backgrounds to why I struggled; missing support due to bias is worse than a few unnecessary contacts or total missed cases.
S1.notes.Q6: As someone who struggled after the switch, immediate personalized feedback could have saved me time and money on moving schools.
S1.notes.Q7: Generic emails are noise; if I get a tailored message saying 'Your lab grades suggest you need tutoring,' that's enough to act without being overwhelmed by mass outreach.

S2.notes.Q3: I am already struggling balancing work and studies. Course performance data is useful because it reflects my current load, but I feel very uneasy about tracking page views or Absalon activity—that feels like constant surveillance. Sensitive personal data (race, gender) crosses a line for me; only disability info might be okay if there's proof of need.
S2.notes.Q4: Trust is everything with an advisor. If I'm flagged, I need to know exactly why so I can address it. Black box models feel alienating and scary. High explainability feels necessary before we flag anyone.
S2.notes.Q5: Missing students from disadvantaged backgrounds hurts me personally as an international student working part-time, but I also don't want to accidentally contact people who are fine just because the model has bias against them.
S2.notes.Q6: Being proactive is better than waiting until I'm in trouble again, but it shouldn't be spammy.
S2.notes.Q7: General emails are harmless noise; personalized ones need careful targeting to avoid harassment or making people feel judged for needing help.

S3.notes.Q3: I can accept grades and school data if they help a lot (large/improve fairness), but page views from Absalon feel like surveillance of my health condition, so never for that. Sensitive disability data is risky unless it specifically targets me or similar conditions without general discrimination.
S3.notes.Q4: As a health student with specific needs, I need to know exactly why I'm being contacted. A 'black box' is scary; if they can't explain it simply, I won't trust them.
S3.notes.Q5: Being a minority and having health issues makes me fear missing help due to bias. If the model misses my potential needs because it assumes everyone with disabilities is fine, that's worse than contacting someone falsely.
S3.notes.Q6: Since my course load changed due to health, I might be struggling right now but don't realize it yet. Waiting a year feels like ignoring immediate crises; timely support is crucial.
S3.notes.Q7: A generic email to many people feels spammy and wasteful for advisors' time. A personalized message or call should go only to those the model has a strong reason (and clear explanation) to flag.
S3.Q8.1: I worry that if I decline help due to fear of bias, data points from my interactions might actually train a biased model against future students like me who also hesitate. We need safe spaces for saying 'no'.

S4.notes.Q3: Course performance is okay because it shows immediate struggle like failing exams or missing deadlines, which explains why I'm struggling right now. Admin data (GPA) feels slightly more retrospective but helpful given my ADHD planning issues; however, online activity and sensitive traits feel too invasive without a major benefit.
S4.notes.Q4: Knowing the specific factors like missing deadlines is crucial because it helps me understand my own pattern of procrastination and seek help for organization, but I worry that a black box model makes advisors look untrustworthy.
S4.notes.Q5: We can't let the system fail to identify my specific demographic if it systematically misses people like me due to bias, even at a slight cost to overall identification numbers.
S4.notes.Q6: If the model spots a pattern of late submissions, I should be contacted immediately rather than waiting for an annual check-up; early intervention is key.
S4.notes.Q7: Personalized outreach feels too intrusive if not perfectly targeted, so I'd rather accept missing a few cases than sending generic emails to everyone flagged.

S5.notes.Q3: Course grades make sense as they reflect my own struggle to adapt here. Admissions data feels intrusive regarding my home country's system. Absalon usage is okay but scary; I'd need better alerts than just 'we noticed you'. Disability and financial aid are sensitive due to stigma.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I am flagged so an advisor can help me fix that specific issue, not just because of a 'pattern'. Without explanation, support is impossible.
S5.notes.Q5: As an international student facing potential bias on campus, missing any struggling students in my group feels unfair to them all. I want everyone identified regardless of their background.
S5.notes.Q6: Generic emails are too impersonal; a personal message or advisor meeting feels safer and more supportive for someone feeling isolated here in Denmark.
S5.notes.Q7: For generic emails, too many cause stress and low trust; for personalized ones where an advisor is involved, the cost of missing a student's crisis might outweigh false positives.

S6.notes.Q3: Course performance is okay if the threshold for flagging people like me isn't too low.

S7.notes.Q3: Course grades make sense for me as a student, but 'Absalon data' (page views) feels like surveillance that breaks the immersion of learning.
S7.notes.Q4: Without knowing the exact reason, I feel panicked if flagged because my dyslexia requires specific accommodations that a black box can't explain.
S7.notes.Q5: Fairness is crucial here; as a disabled student, I worry the model might default to helping those who look like 'average' students rather than needing actual help.
S7.notes.Q6: I think being bothered constantly about my grades is counterproductive to studying; an annual check-in feels more respectful and less like a warning.
S7.notes.Q7: For generic emails, it's annoying but okay if we catch the real cases; for personalized ones with my name and history, I'd hate to be misjudged.

S8.notes.Q3: I'm wary of biometric or sensitive data like nationality due to my Faroese background and past dropout, feeling targeted. Disability is okay if it triggers mandatory help, not just flagging.
S8.notes.Q4: I want clear reasons for flagging; 'black box' models erode trust in support offered to me after leaving a program before.
S8.notes.Q5: Fairness matters more than total numbers, especially for groups historically marginalized by the system or myself.
S8.notes.Q6: Early intervention is crucial to prevent further dropout; generic emails often get ignored, so personalized contact works better.
S8.notes.Q7: With personal outreach, we must be more selective because false positives cause real anxiety and burnout during the semester.

S9.notes.Q3: Course grades help immensely for me; I need that feedback to know if my mental health is affecting my work. But using nationality or race feels invasive and risks bias without adding safety value.
S9.notes.Q4: I need to know exactly why I was flagged, especially if it mentions my disability or mood. A vague algorithm makes me afraid of unfair punishment.
S9.notes.Q5: Missing someone in crisis is worse than annoying an admin by mistake. Fairness must mean catching everyone, even if it costs us some efficiency overall.
S9.notes.Q6: My situation is unstable; waiting for annual checks leaves me exposed. I need support the moment signs appear, regardless of frequency.
S9.notes.Q7: With just an email being sent out constantly would be overwhelming and likely ignored by peers too. Personalized outreach should be reserved for those truly at risk to avoid stigma.
